source_evidence.observation: Elementary operations obey fl(x op y) = (x op y)(1 + δ), |δ| <= u. The paper defines gamma_tilde_n(λ) = exp((λ sqrt(n) u + n u^2)/(1-u)) - 1 = λ sqrt(n) u + O(u^2), λ > 0, and defines mean independence by E(δ_k | δ_{k-1},...,δ_1) = E(δ_k).

The rounding errors are ordered by the computation, satisfy the standard relative-error equation, are mean independent, and each has mean zero. The model does not require full statistical independence.

The matrix concentration result applies to conditionally mean-zero rectangular random matrices with almost-sure quadratic bounds and supplies the tail estimate later used for the sum of the insertion matrices F_j.

The vectors v_i are exact in the first three lemmas. Given P_i = I - v_i v_i^T in R^{m x m}, v_i^T v_i = 2, and b_{j+1} = P_j b_j, the computed result has the perturbed-product representation b_hat_{r+1} = (P_r + ΔP_r)...(P_1 + ΔP_1)b. Simultaneously for all j, ||ΔP_j||_2 <= c_5 gamma_tilde_m(λ) with probability at least 1 - 2rm exp(-λ^2/2).

Lemma 4.2 strengthens the local bound to an almost-sure assumption. Expanding the perturbed product to first order gives b_hat_{r+1} = b_{r+1} + (sum_j P_r...P_{j+1} ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1 + O(u^2))b = b_{r+1} + Q^T(sum_j F_j + O(u^2))b, where F_j = P_1...P_j ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1.

Using computation-order conditioning and Model 1.5, the proof establishes E(F_j | F_{j-1},...,F_1) = 0. With E = sum_j F_j, it obtains ||E||_2 <= c_6 λ sqrt(r) gamma_tilde_m(λ) with probability at least 1 - 2m exp(-λ^2), and consequently b_hat_{r+1} = Q^T(b + Δb) with Δb = Eb + O(u^2).

source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 4.4 proof and higher-order discussion following equation (4.17)
source_evidence.observation: For actual Householder QR, computed Householder-vector errors add only O(u^2) to the local perturbations at this level of analysis. The omitted term in the product expansion consists of terms containing at least two local perturbations; for r = n, its second-order portion contains binomial(n,2) terms.

Ignoring constants and λ, the second-order contribution is bounded by n^2 gamma_tilde_m(λ)^2 ||b||_2, approximately n^2 m u^2 ||b||_2. The first-order dependence is sqrt(mn)u, and the paper requires sqrt(m)n^(3/2)u < 1 for that behavior to dominate; successive higher-order bounds have ratio ((n-k)/(k+1))sqrt(m)u.

binders: m and r are the matrix dimension and number of transformations, with indices i,j = 1:r; no relation such as r <= m is stated for the generic vector result. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1]
For each i = 1:r, v_i is an exact vector in R^m and P_i = I - v_i v_i^T is an m-by-m Householder matrix satisfying v_i^T v_i = 2. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, section 4 preamble and Lemma 4.1]
The exact input is b = b_1 in R^m, with exact iterates b_{j+1} = P_j b_j and b_{r+1} = P_r...P_1 b. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1]
u is the unit roundoff and λ > 0 is the probability parameter appearing in gamma_tilde_m(λ). [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, equations (1.4) and (1.6)]
ΔP_j and F_j are m-by-m random perturbation matrices, E = sum_{j=1}^r F_j, and Δb is a vector in R^m. [PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 1151-1153, equations (4.1), (4.9), and (4.12)-(4.14)]
hypotheses: The algorithm applies the given transformations sequentially as b_{j+1} = b_j - (v_j^T b_j)v_j, j = 1:r, and b_hat_{r+1} denotes its floating-point result. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1]

All primitive rounding errors, in computation order, satisfy fl(x op y) = (x op y)(1 + δ), |δ| <= u, and are mean independent with mean zero. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, equation (1.4), Definition 1.3, and Model 1.5]
Lemma 4.1 gives ||ΔP_j||_2 <= c_5 gamma_tilde_m(λ) simultaneously for every j with probability at least 1 - 2rm exp(-λ^2/2). [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, equations (4.1)-(4.2)]

For Lemma 4.2 and its concentration argument, the bound ||ΔP_j||_2 <= c_5 gamma_tilde_m(λ) is additionally assumed to hold with probability 1 for every j. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, paragraph preceding Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.2]

The insertion matrices are conditionally mean zero: E(F_j | F_{j-1},...,F_1) = 0; this is proved from the ordering of primitive errors and Model 1.5 rather than assumed as independence of the F_j. [PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 1152-1153, proof of Lemma 4.2 and equations (4.10)-(4.11)]
conclusions: The computed result admits b_hat_{r+1} = (P_r + ΔP_r)...(P_1 + ΔP_1)b, with the simultaneous local subordinate-2-norm bound and probability stated above. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, equations (4.1)-(4.2)]
To first order in u, b_hat_{r+1} = b_{r+1} + (sum_{j=1}^r P_r...P_{j+1} ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1 + O(u^2))b. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, first equality in equation (4.8)]

Writing Q = (P_r...P_1)^T and F_j = P_1...P_j ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1, the same expansion is b_hat_{r+1} = b_{r+1} + Q^T(sum_{j=1}^r F_j + O(u^2))b. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, second equality in equation (4.8) and equation (4.9)]

Under the almost-sure local-bound assumption, there exists Δb such that b_hat_{r+1} = Q^T(b + Δb) and ||Δb||_2 <= c_6 λ sqrt(r) gamma_tilde_m(λ)||b||_2 + O(u^2), with probability at least 1 - 2m exp(-λ^2). [PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 1152-1153, equations (4.7) and (4.12)-(4.14)]

The O(u^2) product remainder groups terms containing two or more local perturbations; when r = n, the second-order group has binomial(n,2) terms and is bounded, after omitting constants and λ, by n^2 gamma_tilde_m(λ)^2||b||_2, approximately n^2 m u^2||b||_2. [PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 1154-1155, higher-order discussion following Theorem 4.4]
definitions_and_conventions: The vector 2-norm is ||x||_2 = (x^T x)^(1/2), and the matrix 2-norm is its corresponding subordinate norm. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, paragraph preceding Theorem 1.1]
gamma_tilde_m(λ) = exp((λ sqrt(m)u + m u^2)/(1-u)) - 1 = λ sqrt(m)u + O(u^2). [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, equation (1.6), specialized from n to m]
Mean independence means E(δ_k | δ_{k-1},...,δ_1) = E(δ_k); it is weaker than mutual independence. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, Definition 1.3]
Q = (P_r...P_2P_1)^T, hence Q^T = P_r...P_2P_1 and b_{r+1} = Q^T b. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, Lemma 4.2 and equation (4.8)]
F_j = P_1...P_j ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1 is the conjugated single-perturbation insertion used in the first-order sum. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equation (4.9)]
implicit_context: From P_i = I - v_i v_i^T and v_i^T v_i = 2, one infers P_i^T = P_i and P_i^2 = I; these cancellations justify factoring the first-order insertions through Q^T in equation (4.8). [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, normalized form in Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equations (4.8)-(4.9)]

The exact-vector assumption is explicit for Lemmas 4.1-4.3; computed Householder vectors arise only in the subsequent QR specialization and contribute an additional O(u^2) perturbation. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, section 4 preamble; PDF p. 9, printed p. 1154, Theorem 4.4 proof]

The matrix concentration theorem is invoked with X_j = F_j and almost-sure norm controls to obtain square-root growth in r. [PDF p. 5, printed p. 1150, Theorem 3.2; PDF p. 8, printed p. 1153, equations (4.12)-(4.13)]

The generic vector result permits an arbitrary count r; r is set equal to n only in the later Householder-QR discussion. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 9, printed p. 1154, higher-order discussion]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The claim concerns the standard sequential application of given, exactly normalized Householder matrices to one vector: each step computes the inner product v_j^T b_j, scales v_j, and subtracts it from b_j. It is then used column by column for a matrix and specialized later to Householder QR; it is not the separate right-to-left algorithm for explicitly forming Q. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, section 4 preamble and Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 9, printed p. 1154, Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.4]
numerical_model: Each elementary floating-point operation has a relative error bounded by u: fl(x op y) = (x op y)(1 + δ). [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, equation (1.4)]
The primitive errors are ordered exactly as generated by the computation, are mean independent, and have zero mean. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 1148, Model 1.5]

The dot-product error is represented by a diagonal D_j whose entries are products of m factors 1 + δ, while scaling and subtraction errors are represented by diagonal matrices Lambda_1^(j) and Lambda_2^(j); Lambda_1^(j) may depend on Lambda_2^(j). [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, proof of Lemma 4.1 and equation (4.3)]

No particular floating-point format or rounding mode is imposed by the theorem beyond Model 1.5; the paper says round-to-nearest can violate the model, whereas stochastic rounding satisfies it. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 1148, discussion following Model 1.5]
error_notions: ΔP_j is a local normwise matrix perturbation representing the rounded jth Householder application. [PDF pp. 6-7, printed pp. 1151-1152, equations (4.1)-(4.6)]
Equation (4.8) is a first-order expansion of the forward difference between the computed output b_hat_{r+1} and the exact output b_{r+1}. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equation (4.8)]

Equation (4.7) re-expresses that forward error as a normwise backward error Δb in the input to the exact orthogonal transformation Q^T. [PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 1152-1153, equations (4.7) and (4.14)]
The result is normwise and probabilistic; it is not a componentwise or deterministic all-orders error bound. [PDF pp. 7-10, printed pp. 1152-1155, Lemma 4.2 and higher-order discussion]
norms: For vectors, ||.||_2 is the Euclidean norm; for matrices, ||.||_2 is the subordinate spectral norm. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, norm definitions]
Orthogonality of the exact Householder factors gives ||F_j||_2 = ||ΔP_j||_2, which is used in the concentration estimate. [PDF p. 8, printed p. 1153, paragraph preceding equation (4.12)]
constants_and_indexing: c_5 and c_6 are unspecified integer constants of modest size; the paper supplies no exact numerical values. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, constants convention; PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 1151-1153, equations (4.2) and (4.7)]

Products act in the written order: P_1 acts first on b, and the first-order term for perturbation j has exact factors P_r...P_{j+1} on its left and P_{j-1}...P_1 on its right. [PDF pp. 6-7, printed pp. 1151-1152, Lemma 4.1 and equation (4.8)]

The local bound is simultaneous over j = 1:r with probability at least 1 - 2rm exp(-λ^2/2), while the final backward bound under the strengthened assumption has probability at least 1 - 2m exp(-λ^2). [PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 1151-1153, equations (4.2), (4.7), and (4.13)]

The generic lemma does not assume r = n or m >= n; those relations enter only when specializing to QR factorization. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1; PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 1154-1155, Theorem 4.4 and higher-order discussion]
higher_order_terms: The O(u^2) matrix in equation (4.8) collects all product-expansion terms containing at least two ΔP factors; the displayed sum retains exactly one local perturbation at a time. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equation (4.8); PDF p. 9, printed p. 1154, higher-order discussion]

For r = n, the second-order group has binomial(n,2) terms and is bounded, with constants and λ omitted, by n^2 gamma_tilde_m(λ)^2||b||_2, approximately n^2 m u^2||b||_2. [PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 1154-1155, higher-order discussion following Theorem 4.4]

The first-order dependence is sqrt(mn)u and the second-order dependence is m n^2 u^2, so the paper imposes sqrt(m)n^(3/2)u < 1 for the first-order behavior to dominate. [PDF p. 10, printed p. 1155, equation (4.18) and surrounding discussion]

For k >= 2, the ratio of the bound for order k+1 to that for order k is ((n-k)/(k+1))sqrt(m)u, which is less than one under equation (4.18). [PDF p. 10, printed p. 1155, higher-order ratio calculation]

In the QR specialization, errors in computing v_j add a perturbation of order u c_4 gamma_tilde_m(λ) = O(u^2) to ΔP_j and therefore do not change the stated first-order bound. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 1154, Theorem 4.4 proof]
exceptional_values: Model 1.5 does not explicitly discuss overflow, gradual underflow, subnormal results, NaNs, infinities, or division exceptions; it assumes throughout that the relative-error equation (1.4) applies. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, equation (1.4) and Model 1.5]
The normalization v_i^T v_i = 2 excludes a zero Householder vector in Lemma 4.1. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1]

undebatable_constraints: The matrices in the selected vector result are given exact Householder matrices P_i = I - v_i v_i^T with v_i^T v_i = 2; replacing them by arbitrary matrices or computed v_i changes the stated result. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, section 4 preamble and Lemma 4.1]
The algorithmic order is P_1 first through P_r last, producing b_{r+1} = P_r...P_1b. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1]
The perturbed-product representation contains one local perturbation ΔP_j per computed step and preserves the product order. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, equation (4.1)]
The displayed first-order insertion for index j is P_r...P_{j+1} ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1, and its factored form uses F_j = P_1...P_j ΔP_j P_{j-1}...P_1. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equations (4.8)-(4.9)]

The primitive rounding errors are mean independent and zero mean in computation order; full independence must not be substituted for, or inferred from, this condition. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, Definition 1.3 and Model 1.5]

Lemma 4.2 requires the local norm bound to hold with probability 1, even though Lemma 4.1 proves it only with probability at least 1 - 2rm exp(-λ^2/2). [PDF pp. 6-7, printed pp. 1151-1152, equation (4.2) and Lemma 4.2]

The backward-error conclusion is ||Δb||_2 <= c_6 λ sqrt(r) gamma_tilde_m(λ)||b||_2 + O(u^2), with probability at least 1 - 2m exp(-λ^2). [PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 1152-1153, equations (4.7) and (4.14)]

The O(u^2) remainder must retain all terms with two or more local perturbations; it cannot be silently discarded in an exact formal equality. [PDF pp. 7 and 9, printed pp. 1152 and 1154, equation (4.8) and higher-order discussion]
The generic vector claim has r transformations and does not itself impose the later QR specialization r = n. [PDF p. 6, printed p. 1151, Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 9, printed p. 1154, higher-order discussion]

ambiguities.issue: The notation O(u^2) is not defined as an explicit matrix or vector remainder with a quantified constant or uniformity regime. [PDF pp. 7-10, printed pp. 1152-1155, equations (4.7)-(4.8) and higher-order discussion]
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (4.8) places O(u^2) inside a matrix expression before multiplication by b, while equations (4.7) and (4.14) append O(u^2) to a scalar norm bound; the later discussion supplies order estimates but no formal remainder definition. [PDF pp. 7-10, printed pp. 1152-1155, equations (4.7), (4.8), (4.14), and (4.18)]
ambiguities.impact: An exact formal statement must introduce and quantify a remainder of the appropriate type rather than interpret the displayed big-O equality literally. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equation (4.8)]

ambiguities.issue: The almost-sure local-bound hypothesis of Lemma 4.2 is stronger than the probabilistic conclusion actually established by Lemma 4.1. [PDF pp. 6-7, printed pp. 1151-1152, equations (4.2), (4.6), and Lemma 4.2]
ambiguities.evidence: Lemma 4.1 gives probability 1 - 2rm exp(-λ^2/2), whereas the remaining results explicitly assume probability 1; the authors later acknowledge this replacement. [PDF p. 10, printed p. 1155, paragraph following equation (4.19)]
ambiguities.impact: The probability-one condition must remain an assumption of the enclosing lemma and cannot be claimed as a consequence of Model 1.5 alone. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, Lemma 4.2]

ambiguities.issue: Endpoint empty products are used but not explicitly defined. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equations (4.8)-(4.9)]
ambiguities.evidence: At j = r, P_r...P_{j+1} has no factors; at j = 1, P_{j-1}...P_1 has no factors. The paper relies on the standard identity-matrix convention without stating it. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equations (4.8)-(4.9)]
ambiguities.impact: A formal version must specify that these endpoint products equal the m-by-m identity. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 1152, equations (4.8)-(4.9)]

ambiguities.issue: The constants c_5 and c_6 are intentionally unspecified. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, constants convention; PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 1151-1153, equations (4.2) and (4.7)]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper describes all c_i as integer constants of modest size but does not assign values to c_5 or c_6. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 1147, paragraph preceding Theorem 1.1]
ambiguities.impact: A contract may quantify suitable constants but cannot attribute specific numerical values to them from this passage. [PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 1151-1153, equations (4.2), (4.7), and (4.13)]

ambiguities.issue: Model 1.5 does not select a unique rounding mode or probability distribution. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 1148, Model 1.5 and following discussion]
ambiguities.evidence: Only bounded relative errors, computation-order mean independence, and zero means are required; round-to-nearest is said sometimes to violate the model, while stochastic rounding satisfies it. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 1148, discussion following Model 1.5]
ambiguities.impact: No stronger distributional assumption, identical distribution, mutual independence, or mandatory round-to-nearest semantics may be added. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, Definition 1.3 and Model 1.5]

ambiguities.issue: Exceptional floating-point values and range errors are outside the explicit model. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, equation (1.4) and Model 1.5]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper assumes the relative-error formula and does not state conventions for overflow, underflow, subnormals, infinities, or NaNs in the selected context. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, equation (1.4) and Model 1.5]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must either assume such exceptions do not occur or separately define their treatment; the paper does not resolve that choice. [PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 1147-1148, equation (1.4) and Model 1.5]

contract_plain_english: Given r exact, normalized m-by-m Householder transformations and an exact input vector b, apply the transformations sequentially in floating-point arithmetic whose ordered primitive errors are bounded by u, mean independent, and zero mean. The computed output is exactly representable as a product of locally perturbed Householder matrices. Expanding that product to first order yields the exact output plus the sum of all single-perturbation insertions, equivalently Q^T times the sum of F_j, while every term containing at least two local perturbations is retained as O(u^2). Under the additional assumption that every local spectral-norm bound holds almost surely, matrix concentration gives a backward perturbation Δb bounded by c_6 λ sqrt(r) gamma_tilde_m(λ)||b||_2 + O(u^2) with probability at least 1 - 2m exp(-λ^2). The paper does not provide a formally quantified big-O remainder, numerical values for c_5 or c_6, or exceptional-value semantics. [PDF pp. 2-3 and 6-10, printed pp. 1147-1148 and 1151-1155, equations (1.4), (1.6), (4.1)-(4.2), (4.7)-(4.9), and higher-order discussion following Theorem 4.4]
